title: Bayline Rail Interchange
event: Storm surge and drainage failure flood the rail interchange connecting coastal terminals to inland routes.
why: An interchange sorts and transfers rail cars between routes. Flooding at one interchange can block cargo from several terminals even when inland tracks remain usable.
how: Trains stop outside the flooded area, yards fill, crews lose access, and heavy freight shifts toward roads with less carrying capacity.
when: The risk rises near high tide, during prolonged rainfall, when pumps lose power, or when alternate yards are already receiving diverted trains.
where: The flooding begins near the coast and spreads through port, refinery, warehouse, agricultural, and construction supply chains.

keyTerms.definition: A location where rail cars or trains transfer between routes or railroad networks.
keyTerms.example: Cars arriving from a port are reorganized into trains bound for inland destinations.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: One interchange can connect several cargo sources to a much larger inland network.

keyTerms.definition: A temporary restriction on accepting specified rail traffic when a route or destination cannot handle it safely.
keyTerms.example: A railroad stops accepting new cars for a flooded coastal destination.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: A targeted embargo prevents more equipment from entering a growing queue.

keyTerms.definition: Moving cargo between transportation modes such as rail and truck without changing the cargo itself.
keyTerms.example: A container is lifted from a rail car onto a truck chassis.
keyTerms.whyItMatters: Transfers can preserve movement, but only when equipment, drivers, roads, and terminal capacity are available.

question: Which response best limits the rail backlog without creating a road-capacity failure?
options: Apply a targeted embargo, verify an inland bypass, and transfer only priority cargo to trucks
Move every rail shipment to trucks immediately
Keep accepting trains into the flooded interchange
optionRationales: This response limits the incoming queue, uses a verified rail alternative, and protects road capacity for the most important loads.
The road network, drivers, chassis, and terminals may not have enough capacity for every displaced rail shipment.
Accepting more trains adds congestion and equipment to a location that cannot process them safely.
takeaway: Diversion works when incoming volume is controlled and each alternate mode is checked for capacity.
responsePrinciple: Stop adding to the queue, verify bypass capacity, and transfer only consequence-based priority loads.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: The train stopped before entering the flooded interchange.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: A verified inland rail bypass accepted the priority cars.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: The train remains in a growing queue without a confirmed bypass.

logisticsEffects.activeReason: Rail diversions are increasing demand for trucks and road space.
logisticsEffects.correctReason: Only selected priority loads were transferred to a checked road corridor.
logisticsEffects.incorrectReason: Uncontrolled transfers exceeded available road and truck capacity.

cascadeSteps: Storm surge floods the coastal rail interchange.
Trains stop while yards, crews, and equipment lose access.
Cargo shifts toward inland bypasses and roads with limited capacity.
Energy, agriculture, construction, and retail deliveries arrive late.
